claim: AP2 dwells in a closed, inactive state in the cytosol.
source: AP2 dwells in a closed, inactive state in the cytosol, but adopts an open, active conformation on the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known property of AP2.

claim: AP2 adopts an open, active conformation on the plasma membrane.
source: AP2 dwells in a closed, inactive state in the cytosol, but adopts an open, active conformation on the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known property of AP2.

claim: Membrane-activated AP2 complexes are phosphorylated.
source: Membrane-activated complexes are also phosphorylated, but the significance of this mark is debated.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established observation.

claim: NECAP negatively regulates AP2 by binding open and phosphorylated complexes.
source: We recently proposed that NECAP negatively regulates AP2 by binding open and phosphorylated complexes (Beacham et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The site of AP2 phosphorylation is directly coordinated by residues of the NECAP PHear domain.
source: The site of AP2 phosphorylation is directly coordinated by residues of the NECAP PHear domain that are predicted from genetic screens in C. elegans.
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM structure and genetic screens described in the manuscript.

claim: A second domain of NECAP binds open AP2 complexes generated using membrane mimetics.
source: Using membrane mimetics to generate conformationally open AP2, we find that a second domain of NECAP binds these complexes and cryo-EM reveals both domains of NECAP engaging closed, inactive AP2.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data using membrane mimetics and cryo-EM structures.

claim: Both domains of NECAP cooperate to inactivate AP2.
source: Assays in vitro and in vivo confirm these domains cooperate to inactivate AP2.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro and in vivo assays described in the manuscript.

claim: Phosphorylation marks adaptors for inactivation.
source: We propose that phosphorylation marks adaptors for inactivation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented.

claim: AP2 functions during the earliest stages of clathrin-mediated endocytosis.
source: This process is orchestrated by the clathrin Adaptor Protein two complex (AP2), which interacts with much of the endocytic machinery and functions during the earliest stages of CME (Mettlen et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: Inactive, closed AP2 is initially recruited to the cytosolic face of the plasma membrane through its interaction with PIP2.
source: Inactive, closed AP2 is initially recruited to the cytosolic face of the plasma membrane through its interaction with PhosphatidylInositol-4,5-bisPhosphate (PIP2) (Collins et al., 2002; Höning et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Conformational rearrangement of AP2 to an active, open conformation is promoted by membrane-associated muniscin proteins.
source: At the plasma membrane, conformational rearrangement of AP2 to an active, open conformation is promoted by membrane-associated muniscin proteins (Henne et al., 2010; Hollopeter et al., 2014; Umasankar et al., 2014) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Conversion of AP2 to the open conformation exposes a second binding site for PIP2 that stabilizes membrane engagement.
source: Conversion of AP2 to the open conformation exposes a second binding site for PIP2 that stabilizes membrane engagement (Kadlecova et al., 2017), and also reveals binding sites for clathrin and membrane-embedded cargo (Jackson et al., 2010; Kelly et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Conversion of AP2 to the open conformation reveals binding sites for clathrin and membrane-embedded cargo.
source: Conversion of AP2 to the open conformation exposes a second binding site for PIP2 that stabilizes membrane engagement (Kadlecova et al., 2017), and also reveals binding sites for clathrin and membrane-embedded cargo (Jackson et al., 2010; Kelly et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: AP2 functions as the central regulatory hub of clathrin-coated vesicle formation.
source: These interactions allow AP2 to function as the central regulatory hub of clathrin-coated vesicle formation (Kirchhausen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: NECAPPHear is necessary and sufficient to bind phosphorylated AP2 in vitro.
source: Our analysis showed that NECAPPHear is necessary and sufficient to bind phosphorylated AP2 in vitro (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by pulldown assay data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The cryo-EM structure of phosphorylated AP2 core bound to full-length NECAP2 was determined at approximately 3.2 Å resolution.
source: Here, we report high-resolution cryo-EM structures of NECAP bound to phosphorylated AP2.
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM data and structure determination described in the manuscript.

claim: In the phosphoAP2-NECAP structure, AP2 has adopted a conformation similar to the crystal structure of the closed complex.
source: Globally, AP2 has adopted a conformation similar to the crystal structure of the closed complex (PDB 2VGL; Figure 1—figure supplement 2A) (Collins et al., 2002), which is inactive due to the occlusion of binding sites for cargo and the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of the cryo-EM structure to the crystal structure.

claim: Residues in NECAPPHear interact directly with the phosphorylated mu T156.
source: Our structure is of sufficient quality to build a near-complete molecular model for the phosphoAP2-NECAP complex, which shows that residues in NECAPPHear interact directly with the phosphorylated mu T156 (pT156; see Figure 3B below).
evidence: This is supported by the molecular model built from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The phosphorylated AP2 complex can exist in a closed conformation.
source: These data show that the phosphorylated complex can exist in a closed conformation and suggest that the mechanism of NECAP binding to open complexes that are not phosphorylated must be fundamentally different.
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM structure showing closed phosphorylated AP2.

claim: After opening, AP2 is phosphorylated on the mu subunit.
source: After opening, AP2 is phosphorylated on the mu subunit (Conner et al., 2003; Jackson et al., 2003; Pauloin et al., 1982), but the role of this mark remains poorly defined.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Phosphorylation of AP2 enhances binding to PIP2 and cargo.
source: Some data suggest that phosphorylation of AP2 enhances binding to PIP2 and cargo (Fingerhut et al., 2001; Höning et al., 2005; Ricotta et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Mutation of mu T156A or addition of kinase inhibitors inhibit transferrin uptake in tissue culture.
source: Additionally, mutation of the phosphorylated threonine (mu T156A) or addition of kinase inhibitors have been shown to inhibit transferrin uptake in tissue culture (Olusanya et al., 2001), implying that phosphorylation promotes AP2 activity.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: AAK1 phosphorylates AP2 (mu T156) in vitro.
source: Two kinases have been shown to phosphorylate AP2 (mu T156) in vitro: AP2-Associated Kinase (AAK1) (Conner and Schmid, 2002) and cyclin-G associated kinase (GAK) (Umeda et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: GAK phosphorylates AP2 (mu T156) in vitro.
source: Two kinases have been shown to phosphorylate AP2 (mu T156) in vitro: AP2-Associated Kinase (AAK1) (Conner and Schmid, 2002) and cyclin-G associated kinase (GAK) (Umeda et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: AAK1 appears to inhibit endocytosis using in vitro assays.
source: Curiously, studies involving these kinases suggest that phosphorylation may function in an inactivation pathway, as AAK1 appears to inhibit endocytosis using in vitro assays (Conner and Schmid, 2002), and GAK seems to function in vesicle uncoating (Taylor et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: GAK seems to function in vesicle uncoating.
source: Curiously, studies involving these kinases suggest that phosphorylation may function in an inactivation pathway, as AAK1 appears to inhibit endocytosis using in vitro assays (Conner and Schmid, 2002), and GAK seems to function in vesicle uncoating (Taylor et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: High-resolution imaging reveals that many endocytic pits abort prematurely.
source: High-resolution imaging reveals that many endocytic pits abort prematurely, presumably when a requirement for activation is unmet, such as an absence of PIP2, cargo, or muniscin (Cocucci et al., 2012; Kadlecova et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Adaptor uncoating appears to require PIP2 phosphatase activity.
source: Adaptor uncoating appears to require PIP2 phosphatase activity (Cremona et al., 1999; He et al., 2017), but it is not known whether PIP2 hydrolysis is sufficient to uncoat AP2, as cytosol and ATP are required in vitro (Hannan et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Cytosol and ATP are required for AP2 uncoating in vitro.
source: Adaptor uncoating appears to require PIP2 phosphatase activity (Cremona et al., 1999; He et al., 2017), but it is not known whether PIP2 hydrolysis is sufficient to uncoat AP2, as cytosol and ATP are required in vitro (Hannan et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: NECAP acts as a negative regulator of AP2 in vivo.
source: We recently found that NECAP appears to act as a negative regulator of AP2 in vivo (Beacham et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: NECAP binds to the alpha appendage and beta linker regions of AP2.
source: NECAP is a coat-associated protein that binds to the alpha appendage and beta linker regions of AP2 to facilitate endocytic accessory protein recruitment to sites of endocytosis (Ritter et al., 2003; Ritter et al., 2004; Ritter et al., 2007; Ritter et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Loss of fcho-1 in C. elegans causes AP2 to dwell in an inactive, closed state.
source: In C. elegans, loss of the muniscin, fcho-1, causes AP2 to dwell in an inactive, closed state (Hollopeter et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: Deletion of ncap-1 in fcho-1 mutants restores AP2 to an active, open and phosphorylated state.
source: Deletion of the gene encoding NECAP (ncap-1) in fcho-1 mutants restores AP2 to an active, open and phosphorylated state, suggesting that NECAP counterbalances AP2 activation.
evidence: This is supported by genetic data in C. elegans.

claim: NECAP binds open and phosphorylated AP2 complexes in vitro.
source: Consistent with this model, NECAP binds open and phosphorylated AP2 complexes in vitro, however it is unclear how NECAP recognizes the open and phosphorylated states and whether NECAP can directly close these complexes.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro binding data.

claim: NECAP clamps AP2 complexes into the closed, inactive conformation.
source: Here, we determined cryo-EM structures of NECAP-AP2 complexes which show that NECAP clamps AP2 complexes into the closed, inactive conformation.
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM structures presented in the manuscript.

claim: The NECAP clamping mechanism requires coincident binding of two domains of NECAP.
source: This mechanism requires coincident binding of two domains of NECAP, one of which confers specificity for open complexes, and another that detects AP2 phosphorylation.
evidence: This is supported by structural and biochemical data in the manuscript.

claim: One domain of NECAP confers specificity for open AP2 complexes.
source: This mechanism requires coincident binding of two domains of NECAP, one of which confers specificity for open complexes, and another that detects AP2 phosphorylation.
evidence: This is supported by structural and biochemical data in the manuscript.

claim: One domain of NECAP detects AP2 phosphorylation.
source: This mechanism requires coincident binding of two domains of NECAP, one of which confers specificity for open complexes, and another that detects AP2 phosphorylation.
evidence: This is supported by structural and biochemical data in the manuscript.

claim: Phosphorylation is a key step in the dynamic regulation of AP2 inactivation.
source: Importantly, the site of AP2 phosphorylation is directly bound by NECAP, defining phosphorylation as a key step in the dynamic regulation of AP2 inactivation.
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM structure showing direct binding of NECAP to phosphorylated T156.

claim: There are two paralogues of NECAP in vertebrates.
source: While there are two paralogues of NECAP in vertebrates, we have previously shown that they function equivalently to bind phosphorylated and open AP2 complexes in vitro and rescue loss of NECAP in C. elegans (Beacham et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The two NECAP paralogues in vertebrates function equivalently to bind phosphorylated and open AP2 complexes in vitro.
source: While there are two paralogues of NECAP in vertebrates, we have previously shown that they function equivalently to bind phosphorylated and open AP2 complexes in vitro and rescue loss of NECAP in C. elegans (Beacham et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The two NECAP paralogues in vertebrates can rescue loss of NECAP in C. elegans.
source: While there are two paralogues of NECAP in vertebrates, we have previously shown that they function equivalently to bind phosphorylated and open AP2 complexes in vitro and rescue loss of NECAP in C. elegans (Beacham et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Mutations of T156 itself disable phosphorylation completely.
source: Mutations of T156 itself disable phosphorylation completely, and the two residues in NECAPPHear (A32 and S87) lie within 10 Å of mu T156, which suggests that they disrupt coordination of the phosphate group and explains how they might break the AP2-NECAP interaction in vivo (throughout the text, all residue numbers are for vertebrate proteins, see Figure 2C for C. elegans equivalents).
evidence: This is based on the structural analysis and known biochemistry of phosphorylation.

claim: NECAP A32 and S87 lie within 10 Å of mu T156.
source: Mutations of T156 itself disable phosphorylation completely, and the two residues in NECAPPHear (A32 and S87) lie within 10 Å of mu T156, which suggests that they disrupt coordination of the phosphate group and explains how they might break the AP2-NECAP interaction in vivo (throughout the text, all residue numbers are for vertebrate proteins, see Figure 2C for C. elegans equivalents).
evidence: This is based on measurements from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: NECAP R112 forms electrostatic interactions with the T156 phosphorylation mark.
source: We also noticed that NECAP R112 forms electrostatic interactions with the T156 phosphorylation mark and may be required for binding (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Mutation of NECAP R112 disrupted binding to phosphoAP2 in vitro.
source: As predicted, mutation of NECAP R112 disrupted binding in vitro, similar to either mutations in the mu linker (T156A) or NECAPPHear (S87N) (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by pulldown assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Mutations in NECAP R112, mu T156A, and NECAP S87N suppressed the morphological and fitness defects of fcho-1 mutants.
source: Consistent with the screen, the mutations suppressed the morphological and fitness defects of fcho-1 mutants, as quantified by the number of days for a population to expand and consume a food source (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by fitness assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: NECAPPHear binding to the phosphorylated threonine dictates AP2 inactivation.
source: Together, our data show that NECAPPHear binding to the phosphorylated threonine dictates AP2 inactivation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined structural, biochemical, and genetic data.

claim: In the open AP2 structure, mu T156 is packed against the beta subunit of AP2.
source: One feature that might prevent NECAPPHear binding to the open conformation is that mu T156 is packed against the beta subunit of AP2 in this structure (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C) (Jackson et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the open AP2 crystal structure.

claim: Release and phosphorylation of the mu linker are important regulatory steps in NECAP recruitment.
source: This suggests that release and phosphorylation of the mu linker are important regulatory steps in NECAP recruitment.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observation that T156 is packed against beta in the open conformation.

claim: Heparin and nucleic acids generated protease-sensitive AP2 complexes, suggesting they stimulated conformational rearrangement to the open state.
source: Indeed, two anionic polymers, heparin and nucleic acids, generated protease-sensitive complexes, suggesting that they stimulated a conformational rearrangement of AP2 to the open state (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by protease sensitivity assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: IP6 blocks the stimulatory effect of DNA on AP2.
source: Importantly, the PIP2 mimetic, inositol hexakisphosphate (IP6), blocks the stimulatory effect of DNA on AP2, and is not sufficient to open the complex itself (Figure 4B), consistent with the model that open AP2 is stabilized by simultaneous engagement of multiple PIP2 binding sites by a contiguous polyanionic substrate.
evidence: This is supported by protease sensitivity assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: IP6 is not sufficient to open the AP2 complex itself.
source: Importantly, the PIP2 mimetic, inositol hexakisphosphate (IP6), blocks the stimulatory effect of DNA on AP2, and is not sufficient to open the complex itself (Figure 4B), consistent with the model that open AP2 is stabilized by simultaneous engagement of multiple PIP2 binding sites by a contiguous polyanionic substrate.
evidence: This is supported by protease sensitivity assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Open AP2 is stabilized by simultaneous engagement of multiple PIP2 binding sites by a contiguous polyanionic substrate.
source: Importantly, the PIP2 mimetic, inositol hexakisphosphate (IP6), blocks the stimulatory effect of DNA on AP2, and is not sufficient to open the complex itself (Figure 4B), consistent with the model that open AP2 is stabilized by simultaneous engagement of multiple PIP2 binding sites by a contiguous polyanionic substrate.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results with IP6 and DNA.

claim: In the absence of a DNA oligo, both mu E302K and wild-type AP2 adopted a conformation that matches the crystal structure of the closed complex.
source: In the absence of a DNA oligo, both mu E302K and wild-type AP2 adopted a conformation that matches the crystal structure of the closed complex (PDB 2VGL; Figure 4C–4E).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM 2D and 3D classification data shown in Figures 4C-4E.

claim: In the presence of a 47 nucleotide DNA, approximately 60% of wild type AP2 particles were open.
source: In the presence of an anionic membrane mimetic (47 nucleotide DNA),~60% of wild type and more than 90% of AP2 (mu E302K) particles were open (Figure 4C–4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM 2D and 3D classification data.

claim: In the presence of a 47 nucleotide DNA, more than 90% of AP2 (mu E302K) particles were open.
source: In the presence of an anionic membrane mimetic (47 nucleotide DNA),~60% of wild type and more than 90% of AP2 (mu E302K) particles were open (Figure 4C–4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM 2D and 3D classification data.

claim: The membrane itself affects the conformational equilibrium of AP2.
source: On the basis of these results we refer to AP2 (mu E302K) in the presence of anionic polymer as 'open AP2' in our experiments. In addition, this cryo-EM data suggests that the membrane itself affects the conformational equilibrium of AP2 and demonstrates that we can control the conformation of AP2 in vitro using a defined chemical substrate.
evidence: This is inferred from the cryo-EM data showing DNA-induced opening of AP2.

claim: NECAP bound open AP2 complexes in the absence of phosphorylation.
source: Using our method to generate open AP2, we confirmed that NECAP bound these complexes in the absence of phosphorylation (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by pulldown assay data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: NECAPEx is necessary and sufficient for binding to open AP2.
source: To identify the domain of NECAP that engages open AP2, we tested NECAP truncations (Figure 1B) and found that NECAPEx was necessary and sufficient for binding (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by pulldown assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Binding of NECAPPHear to AP2 in rat brain lysate is enhanced by the presence of NECAPEx.
source: This supports previous data that binding of NECAPPHear to AP2 in rat brain lysate is enhanced by the presence of NECAPEx (Ritter et al., 2013) and explains why NECAPPHear mutants retain this binding (Beacham et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: The open state of AP2 precedes phosphorylation.
source: Because the open state of AP2 precedes phosphorylation (Conner et al., 2003; Hollopeter et al., 2014), we hypothesize NECAPEx may form an initial priming interaction with open AP2 prior to phosphorylation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: NECAPEx may form an initial priming interaction with open AP2 prior to phosphorylation.
source: Because the open state of AP2 precedes phosphorylation (Conner et al., 2003; Hollopeter et al., 2014), we hypothesize NECAPEx may form an initial priming interaction with open AP2 prior to phosphorylation.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the temporal sequence of AP2 opening and phosphorylation.

claim: A cryo-EM structure of phosphorylated AP2 (mu E302K) bound to full-length NECAP2 in the presence of DNA was determined at approximately 3.5 Å resolution.
source: To visualize NECAP bound to an activated, phosphorylated AP2 complex, we determined a ~ 3.5 Å structure of phosphorylated AP2 (mu E302K) bound to full-length NECAP2 in the presence of an anionic polymer (DNA) (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM data and structure determination described in the manuscript.

claim: In the phosphoAP2 (mu E302K)-NECAP-DNA structure, AP2 was not open, but was in a closed, inactive conformation.
source: In contrast to other AP2 (mu E302K) complexes incubated with DNA, (Figure 4B and E), AP2 was not open, but was in a closed, inactive conformation.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the cryo-EM structure.

claim: In the phosphoAP2 (mu E302K)-NECAP-DNA structure, additional density contacting the beta subunit was observed.
source: However, in this new structure we observed additional density contacting the beta subunit (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the cryo-EM map shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The additional density contacting the beta subunit is contiguous with and extends from the C-terminus of NECAPPHear.
source: Comparing isosurface threshold levels of the unsharpened, refined map clearly shows that this density is contiguous and extends from the C-terminus of NECAPPHear (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), suggesting it represents NECAPEx.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the cryo-EM map shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The 'clamped' phosphoAP2-NECAP structure may represent a post-open, inactive conformation of the AP2 complex.
source: We believe this structure may represent a post-open, inactive conformation of the AP2 complex, corresponding to phospho-AP2 simultaneously bound by NECAP and partially engaged with the membrane via the PIP2 pocket on the alpha subunit.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the structural features observed.

claim: The region with the greatest structural changes between 'unclamped' and 'clamped' structures is the alpha-beta interface.
source: The region with the greatest structural changes is the alpha-beta interface, with several helices in the C-terminus of alpha shifting ~1–3 Å (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on comparison of the two cryo-EM structures.

claim: An alpha helix in beta that is part of the Ex domain binding site appears to partially melt when the Ex domain is bound.
source: Additionally, an alpha helix in beta that is part of the Ex domain binding site appears to partially melt when the Ex domain is bound (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Ordered density for DNA is not seen at any of the known PIP2 binding sites in the 'clamped' structure.
source: Ordered density for DNA is not seen at any of the known PIP2 binding sites, consistent with observations that PIP2 binding sites are not ordered pockets but rather a collection of basic residues that protrude into the solvent (Owen et al., 2004).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the cryo-EM map and comparison to known PIP2 binding characteristics.

claim: phosphoAP2-NECAP binds to the single-stranded DNA construct with an affinity of approximately 60 nM.
source: Notably, phosphoAP2-NECAP binds to the single-stranded DNA construct used in this experiment with an affinity of ~60 nM (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), suggesting that our sample is >95% bound to DNA at the concentrations used to make cryo-EM grids (3 μM protein, 15 μM DNA).
evidence: This is supported by gel shift assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Only the PIP2 binding site on the alpha N-terminus is solvent-exposed in the clamped conformation.
source: Importantly, only the PIP2 binding site on the alpha N-terminus is solvent-exposed in the clamped conformation, so the structural consequences of membrane engagement are fundamentally different in the open (several exposed membrane binding sites) versus the closed (a single membrane binding site) conformations.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The genetic screen identified two mutations in the AP2 alpha and beta subunits that escape inactivation by NECAP and are in close proximity to the NECAPEx binding site.
source: Intriguingly, our genetic screen provided an unexpected insight, as it identified two mutations in the AP2 alpha and beta subunits that escape inactivation by NECAP and are in close proximity to the NECAPEx binding site (Figure 2, Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by the genetic screen data and structural analysis.

claim: Purified AP2 complexes with alpha I470D and beta A447P mutations have reduced affinity for NECAP in vitro.
source: Purified AP2 complexes with these mutations have reduced affinity for NECAP in vitro (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by pulldown depletion assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Mutation of the most conserved residues of the NECAPEx domain results in loss of binding to open AP2.
source: Additionally, mutation of the most conserved residues of the NECAPEx domain results in loss of binding to open AP2 (Figure 6B) (Ritter et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by pulldown depletion assay data shown in Figure 6B and a citation to published work.

claim: Mutations in alpha I470D, beta A447P, and NECAPEx recapitulate the NECAP knockout phenotype in the in vivo fitness assay.
source: All three of these mutations recapitulate the NECAP knockout phenotype in our in vivo fitness assay (Figure 6C), imaging assay (Figure 6D), and protease sensitivity assay (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by fitness assay data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Mutations in alpha I470D, beta A447P, and NECAPEx recapitulate the NECAP knockout phenotype in the imaging assay.
source: All three of these mutations recapitulate the NECAP knockout phenotype in our in vivo fitness assay (Figure 6C), imaging assay (Figure 6D), and protease sensitivity assay (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by imaging assay data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Mutations in alpha I470D, beta A447P, and NECAPEx recapitulate the NECAP knockout phenotype in the protease sensitivity assay.
source: All three of these mutations recapitulate the NECAP knockout phenotype in our in vivo fitness assay (Figure 6C), imaging assay (Figure 6D), and protease sensitivity assay (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by protease sensitivity assay data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: NECAPEx specifically recognizes membrane-activated AP2.
source: These data support the conclusion that NECAPEx specifically recognizes membrane-activated AP2.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined genetic, structural, and biochemical data.

claim: Including NECAP decreases the protease sensitivity of open phosphoAP2, consistent with the closed conformation.
source: We incubated open phosphoAP2 with NECAP and found that including NECAP decreases the protease sensitivity of AP2, consistent with the closed conformation observed in our structure (Figure 7A, top).
evidence: This is supported by protease sensitivity assay data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Both NECAPPHear and NECAPEx are required for NECAP to decrease protease sensitivity of AP2.
source: Additionally, by comparing various truncations of NECAP we found that both NECAPPHear and NECAPEx were required for this activity (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by protease sensitivity assay data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: NECAPPHearEx is sufficient to rescue a NECAP deletion in worms using the whole animal fitness assay.
source: Additionally, we observed that NECAPPHearEx was sufficient to rescue a NECAP deletion in worms using our whole animal fitness assay (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by fitness assay data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: NECAPPHearEx locks AP2 into an inactivated conformation.
source: Taken together, these data show that NECAPPHearEx locks AP2 into an inactivated conformation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined in vitro and in vivo data.

claim: NECAP inactivates AP2 by initially recognizing open, unphosphorylated complexes and promoting the closed, inactive conformation after phosphorylation.
source: Our combination of genetic, biochemical, and structural data supports a mechanism by which NECAP inactivates AP2 by initially recognizing open, unphosphorylated complexes and promoting the closed, inactive conformation after phosphorylation (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the combined data presented in the manuscript.

claim: NECAPTail mediates binding of AP2 through the alpha appendage in vertebrate tissue culture.
source: Previous work in vertebrate tissue culture suggests that NECAPTail mediates binding of AP2 through the alpha appendage (Ritter et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: NECAPTail is poorly conserved in C. elegans.
source: However, NECAPTail is poorly conserved in C. elegans (Figure 1B) and is dispensable for activity in our assays (Figure 7A,B) (Beacham et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by conservation analysis shown in Figure 1B and functional data.

claim: NECAPTail is dispensable for NECAP activity in the assays performed.
source: However, NECAPTail is poorly conserved in C. elegans (Figure 1B) and is dispensable for activity in our assays (Figure 7A,B) (Beacham et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by functional assay data shown in Figures 7A and 7B.

claim: The conserved NECAPPHear and NECAPEx domains cooperate to stabilize the closed conformation of AP2 in a three-step cycle.
source: This suggests that we have found an additional and perhaps more ancient activity of NECAP, by which the conserved NECAPPHear and NECAPEx domains cooperate to stabilize the closed conformation of AP2 in a three-step cycle (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: AP2 complexes are recruited to the plasma membrane where PIP2 and other activators induce the opening and stabilization of the complex.
source: First, AP2 complexes are recruited to the plasma membrane where PIP2 and other activators induce the opening and stabilization of the complex (Höning et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: NECAPEx recognizes open AP2 complexes and binds to the beta subunit, placing NECAPPHear close to AP2 at a high local concentration.
source: Next, NECAPEx recognizes open AP2 complexes and binds to the beta subunit, placing NECAPPHear close to AP2 at a high local concentration.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model based on the structural and biochemical data.

claim: After AP2 phosphorylation, NECAPPHear engages the mu subunit of AP2 to clamp the complex in a state resistant to activation.
source: Finally, after AP2 phosphorylation, NECAPPHear engages the mu subunit of AP2 to clamp the complex in a state resistant to activation (Figure 7).

claim: The clamped AP2-NECAP complex is closed despite the otherwise activating signal of membrane mimetics.
source: Our data confirm this complex is closed despite the otherwise activating signal of membrane mimetics (Figure 5B) and is resistant to proteolysis (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM structure and protease sensitivity assay data.

claim: The inactivation cycle has a strong dependence on phosphorylation of AP2.
source: Importantly, this inactivation cycle has a strong dependence on phosphorylation of AP2 (Figure 3), suggesting that inactivation of AP2 is a tightly regulated mechanism.

claim: Inactivation of AP2 is a tightly regulated mechanism.
source: Importantly, this inactivation cycle has a strong dependence on phosphorylation of AP2 (Figure 3), suggesting that inactivation of AP2 is a tightly regulated mechanism.

claim: Data from vertebrate and C. elegans systems are generally consistent, highlighting the evolutionary conservation of the NECAP-AP2 interaction.
source: In general, data from our vertebrate and C. elegans systems are consistent, highlighting the evolutionary conservation of the NECAP-AP2 interaction.
evidence: This is a general observation about the consistency of results across model systems.

claim: NECAP R89 lies only 5 Å from mu pT156.
source: Indeed, NECAP R89 lies only 5 Å from mu pT156, suggesting that it may also contribute to coordination of the phosphorylation mark.

claim: NECAP R89 may contribute to coordination of the phosphorylation mark on mu T156.
source: Indeed, NECAP R89 lies only 5 Å from mu pT156, suggesting that it may also contribute to coordination of the phosphorylation mark.

claim: The R112 mutation appears less potent in C. elegans assays than in pulldowns using vertebrate proteins, possibly due to evolutionary variance in how NECAP recognizes the phosphate on AP2.
source: Additionally, we find that the R112 mutation appears less potent in our C. elegans assays (Figure 2D–F) than in pulldowns using vertebrate proteins (Figure 2C) possibly due to evolutionary variance in how NECAP recognizes the phosphate on AP2.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of results between vertebrate and C. elegans systems.

claim: NECAPPhear binding to phosphoAP2 may not be a major determinant of NECAP binding in vivo.
source: It is possible that NECAPPhear binding to phosphoAP2 is not a major determinant of NECAP binding in vivo.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observation that T156A mutation does not fully abolish NECAP recruitment.

claim: The residual level of NECAP enrichment could be due to an additional interface between NECAP and AP2, such as NECAPEx with AP2 beta or NECAPTail with the AP2 alpha ear.
source: The residual level of NECAP enrichment could be due to an additional interface between NECAP and AP2, such as NECAPEx with AP2 beta (Figure 5) or NECAPTail with the AP2 alpha ear (Ritter et al., 2004).

claim: At low isosurface thresholding, the C-terminus of NECAPPHear appears continuous with the new density assigned to NECAPEx.

claim: There exists the possibility that the density assigned to NECAPEx actually represents DNA or a portion of NECAP bound to DNA.

claim: The active state of AP2 appears to induce phosphorylation in vivo.
source: First, the active state of AP2 appears to induce phosphorylation in vivo, suggesting that AP2 opens on the membrane prior to phosphorylation (Hollopeter et al., 2014).

claim: NECAPEx can engage open AP2 complexes before phosphorylation and subsequent NECAPPHear binding.
source: Thus, NECAPEx can engage open AP2 complexes before phosphorylation and subsequent NECAPPHear binding.

claim: NECAP is observed early at sites of endocytosis.
source: Second, NECAP is observed early at sites of endocytosis (Taylor et al., 2011) and can be incorporated into the coat, apparently without inhibiting pit assembly (Sochacki et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: NECAP can be incorporated into the coat without inhibiting pit assembly.
source: Second, NECAP is observed early at sites of endocytosis (Taylor et al., 2011) and can be incorporated into the coat, apparently without inhibiting pit assembly (Sochacki et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: A priming interaction of NECAPEx with activated AP2 is consistent with early NECAP recruitment and incorporation into the coat without inhibiting pit assembly.
source: A priming interaction of NECAPEx with activated AP2 is consistent with these observations; initially, NECAP is not competent to inactivate AP2, but is poised to do so later in the cycle, after phosphorylation (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is inferred from the proposed model and published observations.

claim: NECAP action may be dictated by the timing of AP2 kinase recruitment or activation.
source: One possibility is that NECAP action is dictated by the timing of AP2 kinase recruitment or activation (Conner et al., 2003; Jackson et al., 2003) and that AP2 complexes become inactivated by NECAP immediately upon phosphorylation.
evidence: This is speculated as one possible mechanism for NECAP regulation.

claim: NECAP may serve as a quality control mechanism by only inactivating AP2 complexes that are not yet fully initiated.
source: Another possibility is that NECAP cannot inactivate stabilized AP2 complexes, but only complexes that are not yet fully initiated, thereby serving as a quality control mechanism (Aguet et al., 2013; Cocucci et al., 2012; Ehrlich et al., 2004; Puthenveedu and von Zastrow, 2006).
evidence: This is speculated as another possible mechanism for NECAP function.

claim: NECAP is reported at endocytic structures coincident with the arrival of clathrin.
source: However, NECAP is reported at endocytic structures (Sochacki et al., 2017) coincident with the arrival of clathrin (Taylor et al., 2011), suggesting that NECAP may act later in the endocytic cycle, after AP2 activation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Clathrin adaptor inactivation may be involved in vesicle uncoating.
source: More speculatively, it is possible that clathrin adaptor inactivation may be involved in vesicle uncoating, as closed AP2 complexes cannot interact with cargo (Collins et al., 2002; Jackson et al., 2010; Kelly et al., 2008) and a clathrin-binding motif on the beta hinge is occluded in this conformation (Kelly et al., 2014).
evidence: This is speculated based on the properties of closed AP2 and cited literature.

claim: Closed AP2 complexes cannot interact with cargo.
source: More speculatively, it is possible that clathrin adaptor inactivation may be involved in vesicle uncoating, as closed AP2 complexes cannot interact with cargo (Collins et al., 2002; Jackson et al., 2010; Kelly et al., 2008) and a clathrin-binding motif on the beta hinge is occluded in this conformation (Kelly et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: A clathrin-binding motif on the beta hinge is occluded in the closed AP2 conformation.

evidence: This is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: AP2 must release NECAP and be dephosphorylated to regenerate the steady-state cytosolic pool.
source: Regardless of when NECAP acts, AP2 must release NECAP and be dephosphorylated to regenerate the steady-state cytosolic pool.
evidence: This is inferred from the need to recycle AP2 to the cytosolic pool.

claim: Another study published during review reports a solution structure of NECAPPHear bound to a fragment of the phosphorylated mu linker that agrees with the cryo-EM structures in this manuscript.
source: During review of this manuscript, another study involving AP2, NECAP, and the role of phosphorylation was published (Wrobel et al., 2019). This study reports a solution structure of NECAPPHear bound to a fragment of the phosphorylated mu linker (AA 149–163) that agrees with our cryo-EM structures.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: The Wrobel et al. study supports the notion that phosphorylation is a key determinant in the timing and action of NECAP in the AP2 regulatory cycle.
source: Their data supports the notion that phosphorylation is a key determinant in the timing and action of NECAP in the AP2 regulatory cycle, a finding generally consistent with this study.
evidence: This is based on comparison with the cited study.

claim: Wrobel et al. propose an activating role for AP2 phosphorylation and NECAP, which directly counters the model in this manuscript.
source: However, Wrobel et al. propose an activating role for AP2 phosphorylation and NECAP, which directly counters our model for NECAP action.
evidence: This is based on comparison with the cited study.

claim: The phosphorylated threonine of the AP2 mu subunit is conserved on the mu subunit of AP1.
source: For example, the phosphorylated threonine of the AP2 mu subunit is conserved on the mu subunit of AP1 (Ghosh and Kornfeld, 2003; Heldwein et al., 2004; Ren et al., 2013) and NECAP has been proposed to both interact with and control AP1 (Chamberland et al., 2016; Ritter et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: NECAP has been proposed to both interact with and control AP1.

evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.
